title: sed Editing Commands & The Hold Space 🧠
description: Use d, a, i, c, and the powerful hold space to perform multi‑line transformations.

slides.title: Basic Line Operations 🛠️
slides.content:
## Delete, Append, Insert, Change

- `d` – delete pattern space; start next cycle.
- `a\` – append text after the line.
- `i\` – insert text before the line.
- `c\` – replace the line(s) with text.

These are the classic `sed` editing commands used with addresses.

quizData.question: Which sed command replaces an entire addressed line?
quizData.explanation: `c\text` changes (replaces) the matched line(s) with the given text.

slides.title: The Pattern Space vs. The Hold Space 🧠
slides.content:
## Dual Buffers

`sed` has two internal buffers:
- **Pattern space** – holds the current line (or lines) being processed.
- **Hold space** – temporary storage that persists across lines.

Commands:
- `h` – copy pattern space to hold space.
- `H` – append pattern space to hold space (with newline).
- `g` – copy hold space to pattern space.
- `G` – append hold space to pattern space (with newline).
- `x` – exchange pattern and hold spaces.

quizData.question: What does `G` do in sed?

options.text: Copy hold space to pattern space
Append hold space to pattern space
Move pattern space to hold space

quizData.explanation: `G` appends the hold space (with a newline) to the pattern space.

slides.title: Multi‑line Joining with `N` 🔗
slides.content:
## Bring Next Line into Pattern Space

`N` reads the next line and appends it to the pattern space (separated by a newline). This lets you process pairs of lines together.

Example: join lines ending with backslash.
```bash
sed ':a;/\\$/N;s/\\\n//;ta'
```

slides.title: Branching with `:` and `t` 🏷️
slides.content:
## Labels and Conditional Jumps

- `:label` – define a label.
- `b label` – unconditional jump.
- `t label` – jump if a substitution was made since last input line or `t`.

This enables loops inside sed, like the backslash‑joining example.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `sed -n '1h;1!H;${g;s/\n/ /g;p}'` to join all lines into one. Hold space accumulates lines, then on last line swap and remove newlines.
